Common questions

Before you call

What does Exio do?
Exio helps owners of private companies build value and sell. It starts with a free dashboard that scores your business. From there you can add advisor time, a story-driven listing with owner video, and a full sale to qualified buyers.
Do I have to talk to someone to get started?
No. Create your free dashboard and you will see your Salability Score right away. When you want an advisor, you book and pay for a session in the dashboard.
How is Exio different from a business broker?
A broker usually writes a teaser and shops it. Exio gives you tools first, then people: a dashboard to build value, advisors when you want them, a listing that leads with your story and video, and a live view of every buyer view, NDA, and request.
What size businesses does Exio work with?
Privately held companies with real revenue, typically valued over $2 million. We do not work with publicly traded companies. Any owner can start with the free dashboard and build toward a sale.
How do buyers see a company's financials?
Public pages never name the company. Buyers create a free buyer dashboard and sign the NDA inside it. The listing advisor reviews each buyer, usually within 24 hours, before private details open. The data room requires a second, exclusive approval.
Can brokers list on Exio?
Yes. Brokers and M&A advisors list client companies through the partner program and manage buyers from the broker portal.

Guides for owners and buyers

FAQ

Straight answers

What is my business worth?
Most lower-middle-market companies sell for a multiple of EBITDA. The multiple depends on salability: owner dependency, customer concentration, recurring revenue, and financial quality. A Salability Report gives you a defensible range.
How long does it take to sell a business?
[Typical timeline from launch to close, once confirmed.]
Will my employees find out?
Public listings never name your company. Buyers sign an NDA before they see identifying details, and your advisor approves each request.
What is an IOI, and how is it different from an LOI?
An indication of interest (IOI) is a non-binding outline of price and terms. A letter of intent (LOI) is more detailed and usually starts exclusive due diligence. Exio buyers can submit an IOI from the listing once they have exclusive access.
What do buyers look for in due diligence?
Three years of P&Ls, balance sheets, and tax returns, plus customer contracts, equipment lists, and employee details. Exio's data room templates organize these by industry.

Exio Premier
Upfront onboarding fee
$11,500

One payment at signing. It buys the listing itself. Before a single buyer sees your business, we build what they will see:

  • Financial recast and market research on your industry and likely buyers
  • A video crew at your location to film you and your business
  • Your listing story: teaser video, owner story video, buyer Q&A video, written narrative, SWOT, and charts
  • A secure data room with three levels of access that you control
  • The first release of your listing to our buyer network
  • A dedicated advisor as needed, and negotiation on your behalf with one of Exio's trusted broker partners

We charge for the build when it happens rather than folding it into a larger fee at closing. That is the trade: you cover the build up front, and our success fee is 1.5% of your sale price instead of the 6% to 12% a traditional brokerage charges.

The bottom line
Keep up to more

selling the same business, at the same price, with Exio instead of a traditional broker

No hidden terms. Ask, and we will send you our actual contract before you ever get on a call with us.
Start free and see if you qualify

Traditional broker fees typically follow an industry-standard sliding scale based on deal size (commonly known as the Lehman formula and its variants), roughly 10% to 12% for deals under $1M, stepping down to 3% to 5% for deals above $50M. Actual rates vary by broker and deal. Exio Premier fee structure: $11,500 onboarding plus a 1.5% success fee at closing. Exio Pro: $1,500 a month plus a 1% success fee at closing. The success fee is calculated on total consideration, which can include seller notes, earnouts, and liabilities assumed by the buyer.
